Hi Lidia,

to verify that you have done it correct, you can always change the
observed data to something else and something you do know, and validate
the predictions there.

yes, if you're predicting a new location you'll need the covariates also
there (or use a model for those as well).

random effects, yes, they will have (likely) mean zero, but will
contribute to the prediction variance.

there is a nice tool in the function, inla.posterior.sample.eval()
which you can use both to extract variables from the simulation and
compute a new statistics. but your case it not to hard to do 'manually'.

All the best
H

messages.body_plain:
The non-indentical results is a feature when running in parallel as Finn
said.

The issue is that the initial value will have a tiny effect of the
obtained mode, and when the initial value is the previous mode obtained
in that thread, then the fine digits are all random.

You can reduce the dependency of running in parallel, lowering the
tolerance, like

	control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-12)

or so. not to worry if the tolerance is to small, as the optimizer will
stop when it cannot improve.

from demo(Bym)

using default values

> r=inla(formula2,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E)
> rr=inla(formula2,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E)
> r$mlik - rr$mlik
                                                  [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration)  1.049806468e-02
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -1.396702828e-06

improved:

> r=inla(formula2,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E,
control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-12))
> rr=inla(formula2,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E,
control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-12))
> r$mlik - rr$mlik
                                                 [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) 1.921693295e-04
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    1.370727205e-06

H

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we have experienced some issues with the parameter 'h', with default
value

	control.inla=list(h=0.01)

and we consider to lower the default value to 0.005 or maybe even to
0.001.

This parameter is the step-size for the hyperparameters when computing
numerical gradients, and sqrt(h) is used for the step-size when
computing the Hessian.

Our concern is that when we're moving to more multi-threaded cases (more
cores, more parallel), then we have recently seen cases where 0.005 is
way better than 0.01, in terms of robustness and the ease of locating
the mode for the hyperparameters.

We would like to know if a change to one of the possible new values
creates issues in your models, either to the better or to the worse.
If would help us very much, if you could try the two new values in your
typical applications, and let us know to either this email, or to
he...@r-inla.org if you are experiencing negative or positive issues wrt
this change. If all is the same as before (I guess this is for almost
all cases!), we do not need any feedback.

Thanks

Håvard & Finn

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

With all the hierarchical model structure, you may instead want to consider not rebalancing the data at all; it’s an approach that is needed for some estimation methods, but it’s really conflating different problems/solutions. Some useful discussion related to this can be found here:

https://www.reddit.com/r/MachineLearning/comments/dzmssp/d_why_does_hierarchical_bayesian_regression_work/

In particular, the reply by “twelveshar”:

The to answer here is also relevant:

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/312780/why-is-accuracy-not-the-best-measure-for-assessing-classification-models/312787#312787

The question you ask about how to modify the graph is part of the answer in the discussions; for both independent and dependent structured random effects, what are you really replicating? All the random components related to the observation, or just the observation itself (I.e. duplicating rows of the data.frame)? The hierarchical model should estimate the imbalance, given the original data. Considerations about how to convert the posterior predictive probabilities is a matter for (bayesian) decision theory, where the decision loss function can take imbalances into account, in how different types of classification error is penalized. (See the second link for more about that)

Finn

I'm stuck on one problem because I'm unable to correctly specify the fixed effect to a lognormal distribution, and I'm getting very different results.

This is the code using rethinking (https://github.com/rmcelreath/statrethinking_winter2019/blob/master/homework/week02_solutions.pdf)

library(rethinking)
data(Howell1)
d <- Howell1
d$log_weight <- log(d$weight)
xbar <- mean(d$log_weight)

m2 <- quap(
alist(
height ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ) ,
mu <- a + b*( log_weight - xbar ) ,
a ~ dnorm( 178 , 20 ) ,
b ~ dlnorm( 0 , 1 ) ,
sigma ~ dunif( 0 , 50 )
), data=d )

precis(m2)

This is my version in INLA:

library(brinla)
library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)
data(Howell1)

log_wplot <- log(1:60)

  mutate(log_weight= log(weight)) %>%
  select(c("log_weight", "height")) %>%
  rbind(new_logw) %>%
  mutate(xbar= mean(log_weight),

bri.hyperpar.summary(m2.i)

Thanks so much!

Hi,

If I understand the "rethinking" code correctly, it's setting a log-normal distribution on "b" itself, but the INLA code you're using is treating b as iid random effects, with a log-Normal prior on the precision parameter of that random effect. (it's not clear to me if "b" in the rethinking code is a single logNormal realisation, or several independent realisations, but that doesn't change much, since it's the distribution itself that's the main issue, but it affects what "idx" needs to be set to)

It's possible to approximate a model where the random effect itself is log-Normal, by using the inlabru package; see inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org>
The syntax for the inlabru formula is a general R expression, so it would look similar to the rethinking code.
It should be something like this:

library(inlabru)
formula <- height ~ a + exp(log_b) * log_w
components <- ~ a + log_b(map = d2.i$idx, model = "iid", hyper=list(theta=list(prior="normal", param = c(0, 1))))
result <- bru(components = components, formula = formula, family = "gaussian", data = d2.i)

inlabru will then iteratively linearise the predictor and run inla on the linearised version.

Finn

Comparison between the clinear and inlabru approaches (one can also use clinear within inlabru; it's a comparison between having log_b be a Gaussian hyperparameter, and having log_b be a latent Gaussian, with iterative linearsiation). The result comparison at the end shows some differences in the results for this small and noisy test example; with more data the differences is reduced.  The clinear approach was fairly sensitive to the h=... setting for the numerical derivatives.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(INLA))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(inlabru))

set.seed(12L)
data <-
  data.frame(a = 5, log_b = rnorm(1), log_w = 1:10) %>%
  mutate(y = a + exp(log_b) * log_w + rnorm(n(), sd = 1))

# inla, clinear (transformed hyperparameter)
formula = y ~ -1 + a + f(log_w, model = "clinear", range=c(0, Inf),
                         hyper=list(theta=list(prior = "normal", param=c(0, 1))))
r1 <- inla(formula = formula,
           data=data,
           control.inla = list(h = 0.0001))

# inlabru, transformed latent Gaussian
components <- ~ -1 + a + log_b(map = 1, model = "iid", n = 1,

                               hyper=list(theta=list(prior="normal", param = c(0, 1))))

formula <- y ~ a + exp(log_b) * log_w
r2 <- bru(components = components, formula = formula, family = "gaussian",
          data = data,
          options = list(control.inla = list(h = 0.0001)))

# Comparison
quant <- c("0.025quant", "0.5quant", "0.975quant")
rbind(
  clinear = cbind("True b" = exp(data$log_b[1]),
                  r1$summary.hyperpar["Beta for log_w", quant]),
  inlabru = cbind("True b" = exp(data$log_b[1]),
                  exp(r2$summary.random$log_b[quant]))
)

Hi all!

It worked!! I got very similar results as using the rethinking package by implementing the clinear strategy (see code below). Thank you all so much for your help!

library(rethinking)

library(brinla)
library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)

data(Howell1)
d <- Howell1
log_wplot <- log(1:60)
new_logw <- bind_cols(log_wplot, NA)
colnames(new_logw) <- c("log_weight", "height")

# add the weight values of interest to the dataframe
d2.i <- d %>%
  mutate(log_weight= log(weight)) %>%
  select(c("log_weight", "height")) %>%
  rbind(new_logw) %>%
  mutate(xbar= mean(log_weight),

         log_w= log_weight - xbar)

m2.i<- inla(height ~ f(log_w, model = "clinear", range=c(0, Inf),
                         hyper=list(theta=list(prior = "normal", param=c(0, 1)))), data= d2.i,

            control.fixed = list(
        mean.intercept= 178,
        prec.intercept= 1/(20^2)),# sd = 20 --> precision =1/variance --> 1/(sd^2)
        control.compute = list(config= TRUE),

        control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
        control.inla = list(h = 0.0001),
        verbose = TRUE
)

summary(m2.i)
bri.hyperpar.summary(m2.i)

nobs <- 100

  data.frame(x = rnorm(nobs),
             mygroup = rep(seq_len(ngroups), nobs / ngroups)) %>%
  mutate(y = rnorm(ngroups)[mygroup] +
           rnorm(ngroups)[mygroup] * x +
           rnorm(nobs, sd = 0.1))
components <- ~ -1 +
  intercept(map = mygroup, model="iid", n = ngroups) +
  betax(map = mygroup, model="iid", n = ngroups)
formula <- y ~ intercept + betax * x
result <- bru(components = components,
              formula = formula,
              family = "gaussian",
              data = as.data.frame(data))
INLA:::summary.inla(result)

messages.subject_clean: Visualization of interaction between fixed effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brigitte,

You can follow the same process, except creating the predictions is a bit more involved.

As far as I understand, your model is a GLMM, with zero-centered, spatially and temporally structured random effects. To explore fixed effects behavior, you can ignore the random effects and make predictions based on the fixed effect estimates. You make a prediction dataset like before. You get fixed effect estimates using inla.posterior.sample().

Below is an example with a simpler GLMM, with only a random intercept. Maybe you can adapt this code to your example.

Best,
Tim

----------

# load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(INLA)

# helper function to get samples from fixed effect posteriors
get_fixed_samples <- function(mod=r1, ss=10) {
  fe <- c(rownames(mod$summary.fixed))
  idx <- as.list(rep(0, length(fe)))
  names(idx) <- fe
  samp <- inla.posterior.sample(n=ss, result=mod, selection=idx)
  samp <- t(as.data.frame(lapply(samp, function(x) x$latent)))
  samp <- as.matrix(as.data.frame(samp))
  colnames(samp) <- fe
  rownames(samp) <- NULL
  return(samp)
}

# make data with random intercept and two interacting continuous fixed effects
ngroups <- 10
nobs <- 100
beta0 <- 5
beta1 <- 1
beta2 <- 2
beta3 <- -3
dat <- data.frame(x1 = runif(nobs, -1, 1),
                   x2 = runif(nobs, -1, 1),
                   mygroup = rep(seq_len(ngroups), nobs / ngroups)) %>%
  mutate(y = beta0 +
           (beta1 * x1) +
           (beta2 * x2) +
           (beta3 * x1 * x2) +
           (rnorm(ngroups)[mygroup]) +
           rnorm(nobs, sd = 0.1),
         x2_cat=factor(cut(x2, breaks = 5)))
summary(dat)

# plot it to see interaction in generated data
ggplot(dat, aes(x1, y, group=mygroup)) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=F) + facet_wrap(~x2_cat)

# run inla model and specify config=T for posterior sampling
form1 <- y ~ 1 + x1 * x2 + f(mygroup, model="iid")
res1 <- inla(form1, data = as.data.frame(dat),
             control.compute=list(config=T))
summary(res1) # looks like mean param estimates match input values

# get samples from fixed effect posteriors
nsim <- 1000
samps <- get_fixed_samples(mod=res1, ss=nsim)

# make prediction covariate matrix that has same columns as sample matrix
newdat <- expand.grid(`(Intercept)`=1,
                      x1=seq(-1, 1, length.out=20),
                      x2=seq(-1, 1, length.out=20)) %>%
  mutate(`x1:x2`=x1 * x2) %>% as.matrix()
head(samps)
head(newdat)

# make matrix for the predictions and fill it
fitmat <- matrix(nrow=nrow(newdat), ncol=nsim)
for(i in 1:nsim) fitmat[,i] <- newdat %*% samps[i,]

# summarize prediction matrix
preds <- as.data.frame(newdat) %>%
  mutate(mean=apply(fitmat, 1, mean),
        lcl=apply(fitmat, 1, quantile, prob=0.025),
        ucl=apply(fitmat, 1, quantile, prob=0.975),
        x2_cat=factor(cut(x2, breaks = 5))) %>%
  arrange(x1)

# plot predictions that demonstrate interaction between fixed effects
ggplot(preds %>% group_by(x1,x2_cat) %>% sample_n(1)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(x=x1, ymin=lcl, ymax=ucl, color=x2_cat), alpha=0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x=x1, y=mean, color=x2_cat), alpha=0.8) # +
  # facet_wrap(~x2_cat)
ggplot(preds, aes(x=x1, y=x2, z=mean)) + geom_contour_filled()

# make an interactive version of the interaction (best viewed in RStudio)
plot_ly() %>% add_surface(x=~unique(preds$x1), y=~unique(preds$x2),
                          z=matrix(preds$mean, nrow=length(unique(preds$x2))))

------

For these particular data, it's probably right that a combination of Bernoulli and Beta is needed. But in more general practice, 0 and 1 outcomes _can_ and do occur in what might otherwise be well approximated by a Beta distribution, due to basic rounding of the recorded measurements, or related discretisation effects, where the 0/1 variables should only really be _close_ to 0/1.  I've been working on a solution to that aspect of the problem (the traditional solutions to that problem can introduce large bias), and Haavard has just this week implemented an experimental version of that solution (I don't think it's even in the built package yet; and even then it should be treated as experimental until we've done more work and writing on it).

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Clarification on combing space and time components
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Clarification on combing space and time components
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the short answer:

Let Cs and Ct be the covariances of a purely spatial model and a purely temporal model.

A model that using two f() components gives a functional additive model,
  \eta(s,t) = f1(s) + f2(t)
and the combined space-time covariance matrix can be written
  C = Ct \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes Cs
i.e. the sum of kronecker products, where 1 are all-one matrices of required size;
the spatial function is constant over time, and the temporal function is constant across space.

A model using a single f() with group gives a joint model
  \eta(s,t) = f(s,t)
with space-time covariance matrix
  C = Ct \otimes Cs

The first version is separable on a functional level.
The second version is only separable on the covariance level.
Both use the same set of parameters (except that the second version only needs one common precision scaling parameter).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] bym2 simulation
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] bym2 simulation
messages.body_plain:
This is a useful trick, as we can make a model with no data and fixed
hyperpar, and then just sample from the posterior = prior in this case.

You have to add something on the diag to make it non-singular though

data(Germany)
g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")

formula = Y ~ -1 + f(region,model="bym2",graph=g,
                     scale.model = TRUE, diagonal = 1E-4,
                     hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 0, fixed =
TRUE),
                                  phi =  list(initial = 0, fixed =
TRUE)))
Germany$Y[] <- NA
r = inla(formula,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E,
         control.compute = list(config = TRUE))

x <- inla.posterior.sample(10, r, num.threads = 1)
fun <- function() return (region)
## each column is a sample
bym2.samples <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x)
dim(bym2.samples)

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what you mean by cpo for m predictions, but yes, you can do "brute force" predictive calculations like this:

Method 1:
Fit model to first 1:n observations, and extract cpo for the n:th observation.
Repeat that for all n.

That would give you full one-step-prediction scores.

If you're ok with using a joint point estimate of the parameters, this is an option:
Method2:
Estimate the full joint model using all data
Do method 1, but with hyperparameters fixed to the joint estimate (the theta-mode or the theta-mean)

A hybrid method is to integrate over the joint hyperparameter posterior:
Method3:
Estimate the full joint model using all data
For each hyperparameter configuration in the "config" output,
  do method 1, but with hyperparameters fixed to one configuration at a time

The log-predictive score for observation n is then

\log p(y_n|y_old) \approx \log \sum_k p(y_n|y_old, theta_k) p(theta_k|y_all)

where p(y_n|y_old, theta_k) is the one-step-prediction density for observation n (as in Method 1)
for a fixed hyperparameter configuration theta_k,
and p(theta_k|y_all) is the posterior density for (the integration weight given in the "config").

Finn

Hi,
you've defined the mesh and model so that it's defined on a region larger than the domain of interest.
This is good, in the sense that it moves SPDE boundary effects away from the region of interest.
If you're only interested in the results over land, then you can simply mask out the points that are over land (I'm guessing from the plots that the are of interest is the ocean, but it's not entirely clear); in the plot, you've calculated the result on a grid that only covers part of the mesh, and what you need to do is just to remove all the points on land.

The benefit of the above approach is that it's easy.
If you need a model that isn't spatially stationary and isotropic, but rather takes into account the complicated archipelago geometry, then you'll want to use the "barrier model" approach, that prohibits dependence across land (if the model is to live on the ocean), see http://www.r-inla.org/barrier-model
For those models, you also need to filter out the locations outside the domain of interest.

Dear Dr Rue and R-INLA users,

I am learning how to use R-INLA to fit different joint models of longitudinal and survival outcomes.

I think I have well understood the example presented in section 10.7.5 (https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-survival.html#joint-model-with-correlated-terms). However, the association structure between the longitudinal and time-to-event traits of this model is based on shared random effects. I am wondering how I can change this association structure for the expected value of the longitudinal trajectory at the current time point (known as "current value" parametrization). Is there some specific options I should use?

Model fitted in section 10.7.5 (shared random effects joint model)
yj∼lognorm(μj,τ), j=1,…,2968

μj=βl,0+βl,t⋅tj+βl,trt⋅trtj+β1,i(j)+β2,i(j)tj

log(λi)=βs,0+βs,trt⋅trti+β1⋅β1,i+β2⋅β2,i⋅ti
